01

Business Understanding

The ExCo is weighing three related decisions. We scope this engagement to the one that the other two sit on top of.

CEO
Return on invested capital
Wants investors funding loans through the platform to earn strong, risk-adjusted returns — which means keeping bad loans out of the funded pool.
CFO
Interest profit
Focused on the interest income Lending Club earns a cut of over the life of each loan — profit that a default erases along with the principal.
CMO
Market share vs. Prosper
Needs a durable growth story: an investor base that trusts the platform's returns is the best lever against competing marketplaces.

Underneath these three goals sit three candidate decisions: which applications to feature to investors, how to price interest rate by risk tier, and which borrower segments to prioritize for growth. We focus this analysis on the first — the screening decision — because it serves all three ExCo members at once: keeping high-risk applications out of the featured pool protects ROIC and interest profit directly, and a track record of solid investor returns is Lending Club's strongest market-share lever. Risk-based pricing and portfolio-level growth targeting both build on the same underlying risk model, and are the subject of Updates 2 and 3.

02

Source of Value

Lending Club's key asset is the historical record of funded loans and what actually happened to them. That record lets us convert experience into a screen for applications that have not funded yet.

STEP 1

Learn

Fit the statistical relationship between borrower/loan attributes known at the time of funding and the eventual default outcome, using the 9,578-loan historical sample.

→
STEP 2

Screen

Score new applications through that learned relationship before they are ever shown to investors, flagging the high-risk ones.

→
STEP 3

Improve

Fewer bad loans funded lifts ROIC and interest profit directly, and a stronger investor track record compounds into market share.

Update 1 does the groundwork for Step 1 — understanding the data and its structure — before Update 2 builds the classification models themselves.

03

Data Understanding

One row is one 3-year loan funded on the platform between May 2007 and February 2010. The critical distinction for any future model is when a field becomes known.

KNOWN AT APPLICATION — usable as predictors

credit.policypurposeint.rateinstallment log.annual.incdtificodays.with.cr.line revol.balrevol.utilinq.last.6mthsdelinq.2yrspub.rec

13 fields the investor already has in hand when deciding whether to fund the loan.

KNOWN ONLY AFTER THE OUTCOME — exclude from modeling

tot.paymentprincipalinterest

Deterministic functions of installment / int.rate and the realized outcome. Using them as predictors would leak the answer into the model — they exist only to compute profit, loss, and ROIC after a screening decision is made.

Which features should matter most for profitability? Before looking at outcomes, industry intuition points to fico (the standard repayment-risk proxy), int.rate (Lending Club's own risk assessment baked into a number), revol.util (over-leverage signal), dti (repayment capacity relative to income), inq.last.6mths (active credit-shopping / financial stress), and purpose (some stated reasons for borrowing are structurally riskier than others). Section 4 tests every one of these hypotheses against the data.

04

Descriptive Analysis

Distributions, correlation structure, and — the question that matters most — how the default rate itself moves with each variable.

4.1 · Shape of the data

Exhibit 1

purpose is dominated by debt consolidation (41%) and an "all other" catch-all (24%); 80.5% of loans pass Lending Club's own credit.policy underwriting screen.

Exhibit 2

revol.bal, dti, days.with.cr.line, and inq.last.6mths are right-skewed with long tails; delinq.2yrs and pub.rec sit at zero for most borrowers, behaving as sparse flags rather than continuous measures. fico, int.rate, and log.annual.inc are closer to bell-shaped.

4.2 · Correlation structure

Exhibit 3

As anticipated by the case: int.rate correlates strongly negative with fico (Lending Club prices risk into the rate) and positive with revol.util (utilization feeds the risk assessment behind the rate). The excluded KPI fields are, by construction, almost perfectly correlated with installment/int.rate — confirming they carry no independent information as predictors.

4.3 · How default rate actually moves

100%-normalized views, so the red band height reads directly as the default rate for that bucket.

Exhibit 4

Default rate against octiles of fico, int.rate, revol.util, inq.last.6mths, dti, and log.annual.inc.

Exhibit 5

Default rate by purpose and by credit.policy.

~7%←~26%
fico — cleanest, most monotonic gradient (top vs. bottom octile)
~5%→~25%
int.rate — mirrors FICO, since rate is set from assessed risk
~13%→~32%
inq.last.6mths — steepest gradient of all; credit-shopping is a strong flag
~11–13%→~22%
revol.util — over-leverage signal, rises at the highest utilization
11.2%vs.27.8%
purpose — major_purchase/credit_card vs. small_business (~2.5x)
13.2%vs.27.8%
credit.policy — pass vs. fail; a real but imperfect filter

dti and log.annual.inc are comparatively flat, with only a mild uptick in the riskiest extreme bin — weaker standalone predictors than the six above. These findings confirm the Section 3 hypotheses and set the variable list for clustering and PCA below.

05

K-Means Clustering

Clustering uses the co-varying patterns among borrower attributes to find naturally occurring segments — independent of the default label itself.

Variables. Nine scaled, continuous, application-time numeric fields: int.rate, installment, log.annual.inc, dti, fico, days.with.cr.line, revol.bal, revol.util, inq.last.6mths. We drop credit.policy (a binary flag downstream of the others, not a continuous attribute) and delinq.2yrs/pub.rec (overwhelmingly zero, Exhibit 2 — near-zero variance that would just add noise to a distance-based method).

Exhibit 6

Elbow (inertia) and silhouette score across k = 2–8. Both curves flatten after k = 4.

Exhibit 7

Standardized cluster centers across all nine clustering variables, used to name each segment.

Silhouette scores stay modest throughout — typical for real borrower data with overlapping, continuous risk gradients rather than tight natural clusters. We proceed with k = 4: few enough to name and act on, while still isolating a distinct high-balance outlier segment.

CLUSTER 1

High-FICO, low-rate safe borrowers

8.8%default
3,074 loans · 32% of book
Lowest int.rate (10%), highest fico (~751), lowest revol.util (~22%) and dti; 95% pass credit.policy.
CLUSTER 2

High-utilization revolvers

18.0%default
2,625 loans · 27% of book
Highest int.rate (14%), highest revol.util (~63%), larger installments, above-average income.
CLUSTER 3

Short-history, small-loan borrowers

20.0%default
3,692 loans · 39% of book — largest segment
Smallest loans (installment ~$210), lowest income, shortest credit history (~3,200 days), lowest fico (~686), highest inq.last.6mths.
CLUSTER 0

High-income jumbo revolvers

28.3%default
187 loans · 2% of book — small outlier segment
Extreme revol.bal (mean ~$191.5k, z ≈ +5.2), highest income, long credit history — yet only 18.7% pass credit.policy, and default the most of any segment.

What this buys us for modeling. Clusters 1–3 line up almost exactly with the archetypes suggested in the case brief. Cluster 0 flags a specific, low-frequency but high-impact risk pattern — a single-variable extreme (revol.bal) that a linear model might under-weight, worth testing as an explicit flag in Update 2. Cluster 3, the largest segment at 39% of volume and above-average risk, is a natural target for tighter screening rules and for the CMO's growth strategy. Segment membership itself could become an engineered categorical feature for the classification models ahead.

06

Principal Component Analysis

A complementary, continuous view to K-means: weighted combinations of the same nine variables that capture the directions of highest variability among loans.

Exhibit 8

PC1 + PC2 explain ~49% of variance; ~6 of 9 components are needed to reach 90% — variance is fairly evenly spread across the nine attributes.

Exhibit 9

Variable loadings across all nine components.

PC1 · 27.0% of variance

Risk / pricing axis

int.rate+0.54
revol.util+0.49
dti+0.31
fico−0.53

High PC1 = higher rate, higher utilization, higher debt-to-income, lower FICO — a riskier borrower. Closely echoes the Exhibit 3 correlation findings.

PC2 · 21.9% of variance · cumulative 49.0%

Scale / establishment axis

log.annual.inc+0.56
installment+0.46
days.with.cr.line+0.46
revol.bal+0.43

High PC2 = higher income, bigger loan, longer credit history, larger absolute balances — a borrower "size"/tenure axis, largely orthogonal to risk.

Exhibit 10

Biplot of PC1 (risk) vs. PC2 (scale), points colored by default, with variable loading vectors overlaid.

Reading the extremes

Highest PC1 (riskiest profile)

int.rate 20.1%, revol.util 99%, fico 672, revol.bal ≈ $952k, a small_business loan that fails credit.policy — exactly the profile PC1 is built to flag, though this loan happened not to default. A reminder that PC1 is a risk tendency, not a certainty. Outcome: paid in full

Lowest PC1 (safest profile)

int.rate 7.1%, revol.util 0.3%, fico 812, dti ≈ 0 — a textbook ultra-safe borrower. Outcome: paid in full

Highest PC2 (largest / most established)

log.annual.inc ≈ 12.77 (~$600k), installment $831.52, revol.bal at the data's maximum ($1,207,359) — a large, established, high-income small_business borrower. Size was not itself protective once PC1-type risk factors were present. Outcome: defaulted

Lowest PC2 (smallest / least established)

Very low reported income (log 7.55, ≈ $1,900/yr — a likely data-quality flag), very short credit history (450 days), high revol.util (87.7%) — a young, short-history, high-utilization borrower.

What this buys us for modeling. PC1 is a ready-made, single-number risk score built purely from unsupervised structure — a useful sanity-check against the logistic regression coefficients in Update 2. The near-orthogonality of PC1 and PC2 suggests risk (int.rate/fico/revol.util/dti) and scale (log.annual.inc/installment/days.with.cr.line/revol.bal) are two largely independent dimensions worth retaining separately, rather than assuming one subsumes the other.

Update 1 · Summary for the ExCo

Three independent lenses converge on the same risk drivers

Correlation analysis, K-means clustering, and PCA were run independently on the same application-time variables — and all three point to the same core set of risk drivers. That convergence is what makes this variable shortlist defensible to carry into Update 2's classification models.

ficoint.raterevol.utildtiinq.last.6mthspurposecredit.policy
Correlation & default-rate analysis

Default rate moves 3–4x across the range of fico, int.rate, revol.util, and inq.last.6mths; purpose and credit.policy are strong categorical splits.

K-means (4 segments)

Safe high-FICO borrowers (32%, 8.8% default) at one end, high-income jumbo revolvers (2%, 28.3% default) at the other — both driven by the same variables.

PCA (2 axes, 49% variance)

A risk/pricing axis and an orthogonal scale/establishment axis, with loadings that mirror the correlation and clustering findings almost exactly.

Bridge to Update 2 — this shortlist, plus the four K-means segments as a candidate engineered feature, defines the variable set for the logistic regression and decision-tree default models next. tot.payment, principal, and interest remain excluded throughout, reserved for computing profit, loss, and ROIC once a screening threshold is chosen in Update 3.
